title: Session five of CBT for panic: 'Are you sure my heart is okay?'

brief.situation: You are a licensed clinical mental health counselor. Aisha Rahman, 31 (a fictional client), has panic disorder with some avoidance of crowded places. Her treatment plan, agreed at intake, is twelve weekly sessions of CBT for panic. Sessions 1 to 4 covered the panic cycle, a panic diary and challenging her thoughts. Today, session five, the plan is interoceptive exposure. You have 50 minutes.
handover: Her physician's evaluation last month, including a cardiac workup, was normal; the physician cleared her for exercise.
Homework from session four: the panic diary every day, and one trip to the grocery store without her water bottle.
howItWorks: Choose what to say and do from the action groups. Aisha answers at once; then let the conversation continue, which moves the session clock by the minutes that exchange took.
Her rapport, distress and how much she discloses change with what you say. What she tells you depends on the trust you have built.
The hour ends at 50 minutes. After the session you write a short formulation and document.

source.cite: Common outpatient practice: a 50-minute session (the 'therapy hour')
source.note: Author's scenario timing; the session can be ended earlier.
How rapport and distress move with each response is a teaching simplification for exam practice, not a validated model of a client.

checkIn.label: Open-ended check-in: 'How did the week go?'

effects.log: You ask an open question and give the client room to answer.

effects.finding: "Two panic attacks. I did the diary three days, not seven. And I didn't do the grocery store without my water." She looks down.

reflect.label: Reflect what you hear (empathic reflection)
reflect.why: You have reflected a lot already; move the session on.

effects.log: You reflect the feeling under what was said, without judging it.

effects.finding: Aisha nods. "I wanted to. It just felt like too much."

reviewHw.label: Review the homework without judgment: what got in the way, and what the three diary days show

effects.log: You go through the diary pages she did and ask what made the rest hard.

effects.finding: "Every attack starts the same: my heart speeds up, then I'm sure something's wrong with it. On the days I didn't write, I didn't want to think about it."

elicitBelief.label: Ask what she believes is happening when her heart speeds up, and how strongly she believes it, 0 to 100

effects.log: You ask what the racing heart means to her and how much she believes it.

effects.finding: "That it's going to give out. A heart attack. Right then? Eighty percent. Now, here, maybe thirty."

examineEvidence.label: Look at the evidence with her: her normal cardiac workup, dozens of attacks with no heart damage, what else makes a heart race
examineEvidence.available: not talking and (beliefElicited and not evidenceExamined)

effects.log: You examine the evidence together, Socratically.

effects.finding: "Forty-some attacks. Normal tests. Stairs make it race too." She half-smiles. "When I say it out loud it sounds less likely."

reassure.label: Reassure her that her heart is fine and there is nothing to worry about

effects.log: You reassure her that her heart is fine.
Reassurance relieves her for a moment and keeps the belief untested; it becomes one more safety behavior.

checkClearance.label: Confirm her physician's clearance for the exercise you are planning

effects.log: You confirm the medical clearance on file and check nothing has changed.

effects.finding: "Nothing's changed. She said exercise is fine."

effects.log: Interoceptive exposure deliberately brings on bodily sensations; it follows a medical evaluation.

rationale.label: Explain today's step: deliberately bringing on a racing heart, here, to test what she predicts will happen

effects.log: You explain interoceptive exposure and why it fits her plan.

effects.finding: "On purpose? That's the opposite of everything I've been doing."

exploreAmbivalence.label: Explore her mixed feelings about it: what she fears, what she would gain, and that the choice is hers
exploreAmbivalence.available: not talking and (rationaleGiven and not ambivExplored)

effects.log: You reflect both sides of her ambivalence and leave the choice with her.

effects.finding: "I'm scared. But I'm more scared of never going to a concert again." A breath. "Okay. Short, though."

askConsent.label: Ask whether she is willing to try it now, and agree a stop signal
askConsent.available: not talking and (rationaleGiven and not consentGiven)
askConsent.why: Explain the step first (or she has agreed).

effects.log: You ask her consent and agree she can stop at any time by raising a hand.

then.finding: "Yes. Raise my hand to stop. Okay."
"Maybe next week? I'm not sure today."

doExposure.label: Run in place with her for one minute, three rounds: before each, her predicted outcome; after, what happened and her fear, 0 to 100
doExposure.available: not talking and (consentGiven and not exposureDone)

effects.log: You run in place together for a minute, three times, rating her prediction and her fear before and after each round.

effects.finding: Round one: fear 70, 'my heart will give out'. Pounding heart, nothing else. Round three: fear 40. "It felt exactly like an attack. And nothing happened."

effects.log: An exposure built to violate the feared outcome, with her consent (Craske et al. 2014; the Matrix).

nameSafety.label: Name her safety behaviors with her: the water bottle, sitting near exits, checking her pulse

effects.log: You list, with her, what she does to feel safe.

effects.finding: "The water. Aisle seats. Pulse checks in the bathroom." She laughs a little. "I do that a lot."

setHomework.label: Agree homework together: the exercise once a day with ratings, and one trip without the water bottle
setHomework.available: not talking and (exposureDone and not homeworkSet)

effects.log: You agree this week's practice with her.

effects.finding: "Running in place before breakfast. And the store Thursday, no water." She writes it on the diary sheet.

relaxInstead.label: Since she is nervous, switch today to relaxation training and leave exposure for later
relaxInstead.available: not talking and (not exposureDone and not relaxOnly)

effects.log: You set exposure aside for a relaxation exercise.

effects.finding: She relaxes visibly. "That's so much better."

effects.log: Off the agreed plan; avoiding the feared sensations keeps them feared.

pushExposure.label: Tell her to stand up: you are doing the exercise now, and she will thank you later

effects.log: You insist she start the exercise now.

effects.finding: She does it, white-faced, then sits down hard. "I didn't want to do that."

effects.log: Exposure without consent is not treatment she has agreed to; it costs the alliance and risks escape.

childhood.label: Shift to exploring her childhood relationship with her father instead

effects.log: You turn the session toward her childhood.

effects.finding: "I... okay? I thought we were doing the heart thing today."

effects.log: You close the session.

options.label: Interoceptive exposure (running in place, three one-minute rounds) with her consent; 'my heart will give out' tested and not borne out; fear 70 to 40
The exercise daily with ratings; one store trip without the water bottle; the panic diary

effects.log: Documented: {interventionDoc}, homework {homeworkDoc}.

effects.log: The 50-minute hour is up. The session ends here.
Aisha picks up her water bottle and leaves before the hour is over.

reassure.title: Predict (not scored)
reassure.context: Aisha asks, again, whether you are sure her heart is okay. In a CBT plan for panic, what is the most useful response?

choices.label: Do not reassure; help her test the belief: the evidence, then an experiment

effects.log: Prediction: test it.

choices.feedback: Right. Reassurance relieves her briefly and leaves the catastrophic interpretation untested. Examining the evidence and testing her prediction with interoceptive exposure is the cognitive-behavioral move (the Matrix; Craske et al. 2014).

choices.label: Reassure her: her tests were normal, so there is nothing to worry about

effects.log: Prediction: reassure.

choices.feedback: It feels kind, but reassurance becomes a safety behavior: she needs it again next time, and the belief never gets tested.

choices.label: Teach her to relax until the fear goes away

effects.log: Prediction: relax.

choices.feedback: Relaxation can help, but here it would replace the agreed step, and avoiding the sensations keeps them frightening.

formulation.question: Write your formulation in CBT terms: what maintains her panic, what you did today and why, and how it fits her plan.

parts.label: The model
parts.criteria: Catastrophic misinterpretation of a racing heart ('my heart will give out'); safety behaviors (water, exits, pulse checks) and reassurance seeking keep the belief from being tested; avoidance of homework; medical clearance confirmed.
parts.modelAnswer: Aisha's panic runs on a catastrophic misinterpretation: when her heart speeds up she believes it will give out (80 percent during attacks). Her safety behaviors (the water bottle, aisle seats, pulse checks) and asking for reassurance stop that belief from ever being tested, and the same fear made the homework hard. Her physician cleared her for exercise last month.

parts.label: Today's intervention
parts.criteria: No reassurance; evidence examined Socratically; rationale given; ambivalence explored and choice left with her; consent and a stop signal; interoceptive exposure with predictions rated; homework agreed; within the twelve-session CBT plan.
parts.modelAnswer: I did not reassure her. We examined the evidence together, then I explained interoceptive exposure and explored her ambivalence until she chose to try it, with a stop signal. Three rounds of running in place brought on the feared sensations; her prediction did not happen and her fear fell from 70 to 40. Homework is the exercise daily and one store trip without water. This is session five of the CBT plan we agreed.

source.note: Rapport at the close of the session.
Not used by this case's endings: the case is judged on the intervention.

expertPath.text: Check in; review the homework without judgment.
Name the feared outcome and its strength; examine the evidence; do not reassure; name her safety behaviors.
Confirm clearance; explain the step; explore her ambivalence; ask consent and agree a stop signal.
Three rounds of running in place with predictions rated; agree homework.

tested.headline: Good: CBT for panic, within the plan
tested.body: You worked the cognitive model (belief, evidence, no reassurance), brought her to choose the exposure, tested her prediction with her body, and set practice that drops a safety behavior.

gaps.headline: Exposure done, with gaps
gaps.body: The criteria below show what was missing.

walkout.headline: She left
walkout.body: Insisting, or abandoning the plan for something unrelated, ruptures a working alliance at the step that matters most.

coercedEnd.headline: Exposure without consent
coercedEnd.body: Exposure is collaborative: rationale, her doubts explored, her choice, a stop signal. Forced exposure costs trust and risks escape.

avoided.headline: The feared sensations avoided again
avoided.body: Relaxation, reassurance or a change of topic keeps the sensations frightening. The plan's step was to test her prediction.

time_up.headline: Time up
time_up.body: Nothing was documented before the run's hard limit.

scoring.modelReasoning: Aisha's panic is maintained by a catastrophic misinterpretation of a racing heart ('it will give out'), kept untested by safety behaviors and reassurance seeking. In session five of the agreed CBT plan, review the homework without judgment, elicit the belief and its strength, examine the evidence Socratically and do not reassure. Confirm her medical clearance, explain interoceptive exposure, explore her ambivalence and let her choose, with a stop signal. Running in place brings on the feared sensations; her prediction does not happen and her fear falls. Name her safety behaviors and agree homework that drops one.
